# Is "Vegetarian diets increase life expectancy vs. meat-eating" false?

**Conclusion: The claim is not false, but it is overstated as a certainty.** The evidence is suggestive and directionally supportive of a mortality benefit from vegetarian/plant-based diets, but effect sizes are modest, evidence quality is rated low-to-moderate, and results vary by outcome and cohort.

## What the evidence shows

**Supportive evidence:** The Adventist Health Study-2, one of the largest cohorts with substantial numbers of vegetarians, found vegetarian diets associated with lower all-cause mortality, with more robust effects in men ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/)). A 2025 meta-analysis of plant-based diet indices similarly reported reduced mortality risk associated with healthful plant-based eating patterns ([frontiersin.org/fnut.2025.1518519](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1518519/full)).

**Mixed/weaker evidence:** A 2021 meta-analysis specifically comparing vegetarian vs. non-vegetarian diets found a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease mortality, but **no significant effect on all-cause mortality**, and explicitly noted the certainty of evidence was low ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/)). A review covering multiple prospective cohorts (Adventist, Oxford, Heidelberg) similarly concluded that "overall mortality is similar for vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians," though vegetarians fared better than the general population ([cambridge.org, Key et al. review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-nutrition-society/article/longterm-health-of-vegetarians-and-vegans/263822873377096A7BAC4F887D42A4CA)).

## Bottom line

The claim isn't false — multiple studies do show associations between vegetarian/plant-based diets and lower mortality, particularly cardiovascular. But it's an oversimplification: at least one rigorous meta-analysis found no significant all-cause mortality benefit, and much evidence comes from observational cohorts (like Adventists) with confounding lifestyle factors (no smoking/alcohol), limiting causal claims about meat-eating specifically.
